title: Modeling long-term trade-offs between single-tree and group selection in uneven-aged mixed forests of Bosnia and Herzegovina
content:
Abstract
The spatial pattern of forest harvesting is important in shaping stand dynamics and ecosystem services. This study evaluates the long-term effects of six spatial harvesting scenarios, ranging from single-tree selection to harvesting gaps of up to 5000 m2 applied within uneven-aged mixed beech-fir-spruce forests in the Dinaric region of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As a diagnostic tool, we employed the tree growth model MOSES (MOdelling Stand rESponse) to assess long-term trends in growing stock, volume increment, merchantable harvest, species composition, carbon stocks, and carbon sequestration under each harvesting scenario. Results of the scenario analysis for the next 100 years suggest that single-tree selection leads to the highest growing stock, merchantable volume, as well as carbon-related measures, and it promotes fir-dominated forests. With increasing group size, management leads to smaller growing stock, but the species balance versus the starting conditions remains stable. In contrast, the harvesting variant of the largest aggregation area with 5000 m2, which may be seen as a shelterwood system, exhibited a declining trend in growing stock and volume increment. Carbon-related measures were primarily shaped by species composition and structural diversity, as stands with a greater broadleaf component tended to store more carbon than conifer-dominated stands. Overall, our study suggests that single-tree selection to small group harvesting (up to1000 m2), which is the prevailing harvesting approach, may support productive and sustainable management of mixed beech–fir–spruce forests in Bosnia and Herzegovina.
